title: Body Systems
subtitle: Signals, balance, reproduction, and systems working together
question: How does your body notice change, send messages, and keep itself in balance?
bigIdea: Multicellular organisms rely on internal systems to survive, reproduce, and interact with their environment.
assessment: Solve a new body case by tracing evidence through two or more systems, then teach the explanation with a labelled model.

lessons.title: The evidence challenge
lessons.question: Can one amazing flight prove a design is best?
lessons.learning: We are learning how a fair comparison and repeated results turn an educated guess into a scientific conclusion.
success: I can make an educated hypothesis with a reason.
I can spot what makes a comparison unfair.
I can use a pattern across repeated trials to revise a claim.
lessons.inquiry: Compare three paper-airplane designs in a fair digital flight test. Run three rounds, use the averages and consistency, and decide which claim the evidence actually supports.
lessons.reflection: What makes an educated guess different from a random guess?
lessons.exit: Write one focused comparison question and identify what you would change, measure, and keep the same.
lessons.evidence: A reasoned prediction, three fair-test corrections, an evidence-based conclusion, and a focused comparison question
lessons.projectContribution: The fair-test and evidence pattern students will reuse when planning their final inquiry.

scenes.label: Predict
scenes.title: Which plane will really fly farthest?
scenes.prompt: Choose a design and give a reason based on what you notice—not on a random guess.
scenes.studentTask: A prediction with one design feature used as a reason

scenes.label: Make it fair
scenes.title: Can we compare these flights fairly?
scenes.prompt: Repair the digital setup, then write the class rules for a fair physical comparison.
scenes.studentTask: A five-rule fair-test agreement

scenes.label: Gather evidence
scenes.title: One spectacular flight is not the whole story
scenes.prompt: Run the physical test and the three digital rounds. Compare the longest flight, average, and consistency.
scenes.studentTask: Nine measurements, averages, and one noticed pattern

scenes.label: Conclude
scenes.title: Make the evidence do the talking
scenes.prompt: Choose the supported claim, critique one limitation, then focus a comparison question of your own.
scenes.studentTask: A claim–evidence–limitation conclusion and one focused question

lessons.title: Reaction-time investigation
lessons.question: How does your body turn a change into an action so quickly?
lessons.learning: We are using reaction-time evidence to explain how receptors, nerves, the brain, and muscles work together.
success: I can collect and compare reaction-time results.
I can trace stimulus → receptor → message → response.
I can explain why reaction time changes from trial to trial.
lessons.inquiry: Collect repeated ruler-drop evidence, compare one safe condition, identify limitations, and build a physical pathway from stimulus to response.
lessons.reflection: Why were your three reaction times not exactly the same?
lessons.exit: Explain one reaction using stimulus → receptor → nerve message → brain/spinal cord → motor message → muscle response.
lessons.evidence: Three reaction-time results, an accurate signal pathway, and one evidence-based explanation
lessons.projectContribution: A complete example of measuring variation and explaining a body-system pathway; saving it to SpacesEDU is optional.

scenes.label: Hook
scenes.title: How fast can your body respond?
scenes.prompt: Use three digital trials to notice variation and generate questions—not to crown the fastest student.
scenes.studentTask: Three anonymous results and two possible reasons for variation

scenes.label: Investigate
scenes.title: Design a fair ruler-drop comparison
scenes.prompt: Collect at least five trials in each condition. Change one safe factor, keep the method consistent, and look for a pattern.
scenes.studentTask: A fair plan, repeated data, average or median, and one limitation

scenes.label: Model
scenes.title: Build the full signal pathway
scenes.prompt: Use six physical cards and the source to trace what happens from the falling ruler to the fingers closing.
scenes.studentTask: A six-part causal pathway with arrows and a model limitation

scenes.label: Explain
scenes.title: What does the evidence actually support?
scenes.prompt: Compare conditions, explain variation, and connect one measured response to the nervous-system pathway.
scenes.studentTask: A claim–evidence–reasoning paragraph or recorded explanation

resources.label: Reaction Time Ruler
resources.task: Identify the signal pathway and one design choice that makes partner trials more consistent.
resources.support: Use the procedure and explanation after students predict. Clarify that the activity measures a response, not a simple reflex.

resources.label: How the Brain and Nervous System Work
resources.task: Add one missing detail to the class pathway and explain what the model still simplifies.
resources.support: Open the nervous-system movie only. Pause after the sensory-message and movement sections.

lessons.title: Case file: too hot, too thirsty
lessons.question: How does your body keep the inside steady when the outside changes?
lessons.learning: We are learning how nervous, hormonal, and excretory systems work together to maintain balance.
success: I can explain homeostasis as active adjustment.
I can describe what kidneys regulate.
I can interpret a simple changing-data graph.
lessons.inquiry: Interpret a fictional hot-practice data set, test model predictions, trace what kidneys keep or remove, and build a feedback loop.
lessons.reflection: Why does keeping balance require conditions to change?
lessons.exit: Use four arrows to explain one hot-day response.
lessons.evidence: A data interpretation and feedback-loop explanation
lessons.projectContribution: A reusable systems explanation showing change → signal → coordinated responses → movement toward balance.

scenes.label: Case
scenes.title: A hot practice
scenes.prompt: Read the timeline and graph before revealing the explanation. Which body response changes first, and what evidence supports your claim?
scenes.studentTask: Three evidence notes and one supported claim about the first response

scenes.label: Model
scenes.title: Change one condition
scenes.prompt: Change heat or water—not both. Predict which responses will change, test the model, and record where it surprises you.
scenes.studentTask: A three-condition comparison table and one model limitation

scenes.label: Kidneys
scenes.title: Keep, return, or remove?
scenes.prompt: Use the source and decision cases to explain how kidneys help regulate blood water and remove wastes.
scenes.learningMode: Source reading · route model · decision cases
scenes.studentTask: A labelled urinary route and three kidney decisions justified with evidence

scenes.label: Explain
scenes.title: Build the feedback loop
scenes.prompt: Arrange change → signal → response → effect → movement toward range, then apply the pattern to a new safe case.
scenes.studentTask: A five-arrow feedback loop and a short explanation of systems working together

resources.label: Your Kidneys and How They Work
resources.source: U.S. National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
resources.task: Find evidence for two things kidneys return to the body and two things they help remove or regulate.
resources.support: Read only the opening diagram and the sections on why kidneys matter and how urine is made. Supply the four key verbs: filter, return, balance, remove.

resources.label: How the Urinary System Works
resources.task: Sketch the route and label which part filters, carries, stores, and releases.
resources.support: Open the urinary-system movie. Pause to add kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra to the route.

lessons.title: Four systems, one body
lessons.question: How can different body systems do different jobs and still act as one connected system?
lessons.learning: We are becoming expert in one body system, then using peer teaching to explain how systems exchange matter or information.
success: I can name the main job and important structures of one system.
I can trace what moves through the system.
I can explain one connection to another system and one limit of a model.
lessons.inquiry: Extract evidence from an approved source, build a route model, teach mixed groups, and solve cross-system cases.
lessons.reflection: What became clearer when another expert connected their system to yours?
lessons.exit: Explain one connection using: when ___ changes, the ___ system sends/moves ___, so the ___ system can ___.
lessons.evidence: An expert route model, a three-minute peer lesson, a four-system comparison, and one cross-system explanation
lessons.projectContribution: A direct rehearsal of the later expert-team structure: learn deeply, teach clearly, answer questions, and revise after feedback.

scenes.label: Become expert
scenes.title: Build one system route
scenes.prompt: Use your assigned source to find the job, structures, what moves, one connection, and one model limit.
scenes.studentTask: Five sourced notes and one route model

scenes.label: Prepare teaching
scenes.title: Make classmates do the thinking
scenes.prompt: Plan a three-minute lesson with one prediction, one visual route, and one check question.
scenes.studentTask: A three-minute interactive expert lesson

scenes.label: Teach
scenes.title: Mixed groups build the whole picture
scenes.prompt: Teach your system, learn the other three, and record one connection after every mini-lesson.
scenes.studentTask: A four-system comparison with three cross-system connections

scenes.label: Transfer
scenes.title: Which systems explain the case?
scenes.prompt: Solve unfamiliar body cases. Select the systems, trace what changes or moves, and defend why one system alone is insufficient.
scenes.studentTask: One multi-system causal explanation and one revision after feedback

resources.label: How the Body Works movie collection
resources.task: Collect evidence for the system's job, important structures, what moves, and one connection to another system.
resources.support: Assign only the brain/nervous, endocrine, or urinary movie that matches each team. Reproductive experts use the teacher-provided district-approved source.

resources.label: Your Endocrine System
resources.task: Explain why hormones are messages and identify one way the nervous and hormonal systems connect.
resources.support: Hormonal experts read the opening and one assigned gland section; do not require memorizing all glands.

lessons.title: Reproduction and development studio
lessons.question: What evidence do we need to explain reproduction, puberty, and development accurately and respectfully?
lessons.learning: We are using accurate biological language and evidence to explain the roles of reproductive structures, cells, hormones, fertilization, and development while recognizing human variation.
success: I can use evidence to identify a structure, cell, or process rather than relying on position or stereotypes.
I can place major events in a simplified sequence and identify what the model leaves out.
I can explain biological function without making assumptions about identity, family role, or every person's development.
lessons.inquiry: Interpret six shuffled evidence cases, build a simplified reproduction-and-development sequence, evaluate puberty claims, and identify model limits.
lessons.reflection: Which statement became more accurate when we changed its wording or added a model limit?
lessons.exit: Use one source-supported fact to explain a structure, cell, process, or variation accurately; students may submit privately.
lessons.evidence: Six evidence-based identifications, an accurate simplified sequence, a source-supported puberty claim, and one explicit model limit
lessons.projectContribution: Accurate foundational knowledge that a later expert team may use; no student must choose this as an inquiry topic or post personal learning publicly.

scenes.label: Learn
scenes.title: Build the foundation before solving
scenes.prompt: Use approved diagrams and precise terms to learn the structures, cells, messages, and basic process. Add anonymous questions without personal disclosure.
scenes.learningMode: Diagram lesson · vocabulary sketch · anonymous questions
scenes.studentTask: A labelled reference page students may keep private

scenes.label: Investigate
scenes.title: Solve the evidence cases
scenes.prompt: The cases and choices are shuffled. Identify the structure, cell, or process and justify it with the strongest clue.
scenes.studentTask: Six identifications with clue-based justifications

scenes.label: Compare
scenes.title: Puberty is a pattern with variation
scenes.prompt: Use two sources to distinguish common patterns from fixed rules, then repair claims that overgeneralize.
scenes.studentTask: Two variation notes and one accurately revised claim

scenes.label: Model
scenes.title: Sequence the process—and name the limits
scenes.prompt: Arrange a simplified path from reproductive cells to early development, then attach warnings about what the model leaves out.
scenes.learningMode: Card sequence · model critique · private exit
scenes.studentTask: A correct sequence, two model limits, and one private or public exit response

resources.label: Physical Development, Ages 11 to 14
resources.task: Find two examples showing that puberty timing, order, or body changes vary, then rewrite one overgeneralized claim.
resources.support: Select short excerpts showing range and variation. Avoid presenting two fixed puberty pathways as descriptions of every student's identity or experience.

resources.label: Your Endocrine System
resources.task: Explain how hormones act as messages without memorizing a list of every gland or hormone.
resources.support: Read the opening explanation of hormones and the teacher-selected puberty section only.

lessons.title: Body systems case conference
lessons.question: Can we explain a new body situation without reducing it to one organ or one system?
lessons.learning: We are combining evidence from nervous, hormonal, excretory, and reproductive systems to build and defend a multi-system explanation.
success: I select systems because the case evidence requires them.
I trace what changes, moves, or is regulated with accurate arrows.
I identify a limit or missing piece instead of pretending the model explains everything.
Our teaching helps classmates reason, not just listen.
lessons.inquiry: Select relevant evidence, build a causal systems model, defend it to a peer panel, and revise one weak connection.
lessons.reflection: Which arrow in our model carries the most explanatory work, and how did feedback improve it?
lessons.exit: Explain one case in five arrows and name one thing the model cannot conclude.
lessons.evidence: A sourced multi-system model, a two-minute defence, a peer question, and one visible revision
lessons.projectContribution: A compact rehearsal for later expert-team inquiry and Minecraft teaching: research enough to explain, build a purposeful model, teach, answer questions, revise, and reflect.

scenes.label: Diagnose
scenes.title: Which evidence matters?
scenes.prompt: Open a fictional case, separate observations from assumptions, and select the systems the evidence actually requires.
scenes.studentTask: A case claim, four evidence notes, and at least two justified systems

scenes.label: Build
scenes.title: Trace the causal system
scenes.prompt: Build arrows from the changing condition through signals, structures, responses, and effects. Add one missing-information marker.
scenes.studentTask: A five-to-eight-arrow causal model with one limitation

scenes.label: Defend
scenes.title: Two-minute case conference
scenes.prompt: Teach the model, answer one challenge question, and record the part classmates found unclear.
scenes.studentTask: A two-minute defence and one evidence-focused question

scenes.label: Revise
scenes.title: Make one high-value improvement
scenes.prompt: Repair the weakest arrow, add missing evidence, or clarify a model limit. Save only if it will genuinely help later inquiry work.
scenes.studentTask: One visible revision and an individual reflection sentence

title: Everyday Mixtures
subtitle: Mystery mixture to local water systems
question: How can a material's properties help us separate a complicated mixture?
assessment: Use material properties to plan, carry out, explain, and evaluate a separation process in a hands-on challenge and a local water-treatment case.

lessons.title: The mystery mixture
lessons.question: How can we identify what is mixed together without guessing?
lessons.learning: We are distinguishing observations from inferences and using material properties as evidence.
success: I record precise observations before naming materials.
I use a test result to support or reject an inference.
I distinguish a heterogeneous mixture from a solution.
lessons.inquiry: Observe the sealed mixture, develop competing inferences, rotate through property tests, and revise the class explanation after viewing and discussing outside examples.
lessons.reflection: Which test changed your thinking most, and why was it stronger than appearance alone?
lessons.exit: Make one claim about a component and support it with a specific test result.
lessons.evidence: A dated notebook page containing observations, two revised inferences, station evidence, and an evidence-based claim
lessons.projectContribution: A reusable inquiry routine: notice carefully, test competing ideas, revise the explanation, and name what the evidence cannot show.

scenes.label: Launch
scenes.title: Build the evidence board
scenes.prompt: Observe the real jar silently, then separate what the class can see from what it is only inferring.
scenes.studentTask: Sketch the jar, record six observations, and add two possible inferences with question marks.

scenes.label: Test
scenes.title: Which properties give useful evidence?
scenes.prompt: Rotate through short tests for magnetism, floating, particle size, and solubility. Use results to revise—not merely confirm—your first ideas.
scenes.studentTask: Complete four property tests and revise at least two inferences in your notebook.

scenes.label: Learn
scenes.title: Mixture, solution, or something else?
scenes.prompt: Use two short videos and the station evidence to strengthen the class model, then test it against unfamiliar examples.
scenes.learningMode: Video · partner concept sort · evidence revision
scenes.studentTask: Annotate the class definition and defend two classifications using observable or testable properties.

scenes.label: Synthesize
scenes.title: What do we know—and what is still hidden?
scenes.prompt: Return to the original jar. Build a supported component list and identify what cannot be confirmed without separating it.
scenes.learningMode: Evidence board · gallery walk · exit claim
scenes.studentTask: Write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph and one unanswered question.

resources.label: The Great Picnic Mix Up
resources.task: Before watching, classify two examples from the jar. During the video, collect one idea that improves the class definition of a mixture or solution, then test that definition against an unfamiliar example.
resources.support: Use the short, accessible explanation as a shared starting point. Keep the thinking at Grade 6 by pausing before examples are classified and requiring students to justify each decision with evidence.

resources.label: Aqueous solutions
resources.task: Use the particle explanation to answer: If salt is invisible in water, what evidence shows that it is still present?
resources.support: Use only solute, solvent, and particles remaining present. Treat electrolytes as an optional curiosity, not required learning.

lessons.title: Separation toolkit lab
lessons.question: Why does each separation method work—and when does it fail?
lessons.learning: We are learning that a method works because of a difference in properties, not because it belongs in a memorized sequence.
success: I connect a method to the property it uses.
I can show what passes through or remains.
I can explain a case in which the method would fail.
lessons.inquiry: Test sieving, magnetism, skimming or decanting, filtration, chromatography, and evaporation; then choose methods for new real-world cases.
lessons.reflection: What property mattered more than the name of the material?
lessons.exit: Choose a method for a new mixture and name one reason it might not fully work.
lessons.evidence: An expert-team demonstration, a six-method comparison chart, and two justified application decisions
lessons.projectContribution: Experience becoming expert on one idea and teaching classmates—an early rehearsal for the later expert-team inquiry.

scenes.label: Question
scenes.title: What must be different for separation to work?
scenes.prompt: Compare six mixture problems and predict which property difference could be useful in each.
scenes.studentTask: Sort six mixture cases by the property difference that might make separation possible.

scenes.label: Investigate
scenes.title: Become the expert on one method
scenes.prompt: Test your assigned method on two suitable mixtures and one difficult case. Find its power and its limit.
scenes.studentTask: Gather evidence from three tests and prepare a three-minute teaching demonstration.

scenes.label: Teach
scenes.title: Build the class separation toolkit
scenes.prompt: Teach your method, watch the other demonstrations, and record what each method separates, leaves behind, and cannot do.
scenes.studentTask: Complete a six-method comparison chart and ask two groups about a limitation.

scenes.label: Apply
scenes.title: Choose a method for a new problem
scenes.prompt: Solve unfamiliar cases such as muddy water, recycling fragments, salt water, and mixed dry foods. Some need more than one step.
scenes.studentTask: Defend two sequences and explain why a tempting alternative would fail.

resources.label: Sugar and Salt Solutions
resources.task: Use evaporation to test the claim that a dissolved substance has disappeared. Record what the model shows and one limitation of the model.
resources.support: Stay on the Macro view first. Use evaporation and concentration; do not assess ions, conductivity, or molarity unless the class asks to extend.

lessons.title: Mixture Rescue Challenge
lessons.question: How much of the mixture can your team recover cleanly?
lessons.learning: We are designing and evaluating a multi-step separation process from evidence.
success: Our sequence is justified by component properties.
We revise the plan when evidence shows a problem.
We evaluate purity, recovery, efficiency, safety, and limitations.
lessons.inquiry: Plan, carry out, critique, and improve a separation sequence using a shared material kit and clear success criteria.
lessons.reflection: Which revision produced the biggest improvement, and what evidence supports that?
lessons.exit: Explain the strongest and weakest part of the team process using property, method, result, and limitation.
lessons.evidence: A justified sequence, safe hands-on process, midpoint revision, recovery result, and an evaluation using at least two criteria
lessons.projectContribution: A complete cycle of planning, testing, feedback, revision, and evaluation that expert teams can reuse later.

scenes.label: Plan
scenes.title: Design the first separation sequence
scenes.prompt: Inspect the tools and sealed sample. Build a sequence that names the property used at every step and predicts what remains mixed.
scenes.studentTask: Create a movable sequence with a because-statement and predicted result for every step.

scenes.label: Test
scenes.title: Run the rescue—and stop halfway
scenes.prompt: Carry out the plan carefully. At the midpoint, compare one result with another team and revise one weak step.
scenes.studentTask: Collect fractions, photograph one problem, receive peer feedback, and revise one step.

scenes.label: Evaluate
scenes.title: How successful was the process?
scenes.prompt: Inspect the final fractions. Score recovery and purity separately, then identify where material was lost or remained mixed.
scenes.learningMode: Evidence inspection · criteria scoring · class comparison
scenes.studentTask: Evaluate the process for purity, recovery, efficiency, and safety using specific evidence.

scenes.label: Explain
scenes.title: Defend one decision and critique another
scenes.prompt: Use scientific language to explain the strongest decision, the weakest decision, and what the team would change next.
scenes.learningMode: Gallery walk · oral defence · notebook reflection
scenes.studentTask: Write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph and respond to a classmate's question.

lessons.title: Where does our water become safe?
lessons.question: How do local water systems combine separation methods—and what can a classroom model not prove?
lessons.learning: We are applying mixture science to a real local system while distinguishing physical separation from disinfection and testing.
success: I can order major treatment and supply steps.
I explain what filtration can and cannot remove.
I identify at least two limits of a classroom filter model.
lessons.inquiry: Trace the local system, extract evidence from a video and map, build a treatment train, test a particle filter, and communicate its limits.
lessons.reflection: Why is 'looks clean' a weak conclusion about drinking water?
lessons.exit: Name one process that removes particles, one process with a different job, and one test still needed.
lessons.evidence: A sourced system diagram, annotated treatment train, filter-model observations, and a public explanation with an explicit safety warning
lessons.projectContribution: A local solutionary-science example connecting physical science, infrastructure, public health, stewardship, and communication.

scenes.label: Trace
scenes.title: Follow one drop to our school
scenes.prompt: Use a local video and system map to trace source, treatment, storage, and delivery. Record evidence rather than copying every detail.
scenes.learningMode: Local video · map reading · partner case file
scenes.studentTask: Build a sourced route diagram with four stages, three jobs, and one uncertainty.

scenes.label: Sequence
scenes.title: Build a treatment train
scenes.prompt: Order process cards so each stage solves a particular water problem. More than one treatment train may be defensible.
scenes.studentTask: Defend the order of a treatment train and explain why filtration alone is insufficient.

scenes.label: Model
scenes.title: What can a classroom filter actually show?
scenes.prompt: Build and test a particle filter. Compare appearance or turbidity before and after, then state what the test cannot establish.
scenes.studentTask: Test one filter design, revise one layer, and compare evidence while keeping the safety warning visible.

scenes.label: Communicate
scenes.title: Correct the dangerous claim
scenes.prompt: Respond to: 'It looks clear, so it is safe to drink.' Create a public explanation that is accurate, concise, and sourced.
scenes.learningMode: Media literacy · choice product · peer review
scenes.studentTask: Create and peer-check a public explanation naming filtration, disinfection or testing, and two model limits.

resources.label: Water resources and filtration-plant field trip
resources.task: Use the official video and map to trace source, treatment, storage, and delivery. Record four system parts, each job, and one question the source does not answer.
resources.support: Show selected chapters rather than the whole resource at once. Pause for route predictions and process-job notes.

resources.label: Where does my water come from?
resources.task: Infer the likely route from watershed to school, marking map evidence and uncertainty separately.
resources.support: Use the map and inquiry questions, not every extension. Model the difference between map evidence and an inference about the school's route.

lessons.title: Learning from place and source
lessons.question: What changes when knowledge is connected to a specific people and place?
lessons.learning: We are learning from a specific source in context and making a careful science connection without treating all First Peoples as one culture.
success: I name who the knowledge comes from and the place it belongs to.
I record only what the source supports.
I can make a science connection without claiming the two knowledge systems are identical.
lessons.inquiry: Read, watch, listen to, or learn directly from one teacher-selected source, then distinguish source-supported learning from a separate science connection.
lessons.reflection: What would be lost if this knowledge were reduced to a generic separation-method label?
lessons.exit: Name the source, one learning it supports, and one thing we should not assume.
lessons.evidence: A correctly attributed source note, specific evidence, a careful science connection, and a clearly stated limit
lessons.projectContribution: One notice and one wonder may be saved to SpacesEDU if useful; this is not a required final-topic choice.

scenes.label: Prepare
scenes.title: Start with the source—not a generic claim
scenes.prompt: Identify who created or shared the source, the Nation or community, the place, and any guidance about sharing.
scenes.studentTask: Record exact attribution, place, purpose, and any protocol or sharing guidance.

scenes.label: Learn
scenes.title: Stay with the source
scenes.prompt: Read, watch, listen, or learn directly. Collect evidence about method, purpose, relationships, and responsibility.
scenes.studentTask: Collect three source-supported details and mark the exact moment, phrase, image, or section that supports each.

scenes.label: Connect
scenes.title: Place two ways of knowing beside each other
scenes.prompt: Separate what the source teaches, a science idea that may connect, and what neither perspective should be made to claim.
scenes.studentTask: Write one sourced learning, one science connection, and one limit or responsibility.

scenes.label: Respond
scenes.title: Return the learning respectfully
scenes.prompt: Choose a brief response that shows accurate listening: a source note, thank-you question, concept sketch, or optional SpacesEDU notice and wonder.
scenes.studentTask: Create a concise response with exact attribution and one question that does not ask the source to represent all peoples.

title: Forces & Motion
subtitle: From everyday motion to safer impacts
question: How can Newton's laws help us reduce harm when motion changes suddenly?
bigIdea: Newton's three laws of motion describe the relationship between force and motion.
assessment: Design, test, and explain a delivery pod that protects a raw egg, using Newton's laws, measured evidence, and visible revision.

lessons.title: Forces readiness check
lessons.question: Which force ideas are ready to use—and which need a quick review?
lessons.learning: We are checking familiar force ideas so the class can spend time investigating rather than repeating secure knowledge.
success: I distinguish motion direction from force direction.
I draw a labelled force arrow on the object receiving the force.
I use evidence to decide whether forces are balanced.
lessons.inquiry: Complete six diagnostic scenarios, repair one explanation, and create a new force-arrow example for a classmate.
lessons.reflection: Which idea changed after the evidence appeared?
lessons.exit: Draw one object, one labelled force arrow, and one sentence explaining whether its motion must change.
lessons.evidence: Six diagnostic responses, one repaired explanation, and one original force-arrow example
lessons.projectContribution: Practice only: force diagrams students will reuse in later investigations and design explanations.

scenes.label: Check
scenes.title: What do we already know?
scenes.prompt: Vote before the explanation appears. Keep your first idea visible so you can notice revision.
scenes.studentTask: Six independent first responses

scenes.label: Review
scenes.title: Use only the clinics we need
scenes.prompt: Join the clinic that matches the evidence, then repair one missed explanation.
scenes.studentTask: One corrected explanation and one labelled model

scenes.label: Decide
scenes.title: Ready to investigate?
scenes.prompt: Use the class evidence to choose the next move, then create one question that would reveal a force pattern.
scenes.studentTask: An exit model and investigation question

lessons.title: Newton's laws in motion
lessons.question: What patterns appear when force, mass, friction, and interactions change?
lessons.learning: We are building Newton's laws from observed patterns before attaching names or formulas.
success: I use repeated evidence to describe a force-and-motion pattern.
I distinguish balanced from unbalanced forces.
I explain action–reaction forces as interactions on two different objects.
I name what a classroom model leaves out.
lessons.inquiry: Rotate through inertia, mass/acceleration, friction, and interaction stations; compare data; then defend which law best explains a new case.
lessons.reflection: Which station made one of Newton's laws feel less like a rule to memorize and more like a pattern?
lessons.exit: Choose one unfamiliar motion and explain it with a force diagram, a Newton pattern, and a model limitation.
lessons.evidence: Four station records, one simple graph, one law-to-case defence, and one model limitation
lessons.projectContribution: A reusable evidence pattern for explaining why a later design changes motion or impact.
lessons.spacesPrompt: Optional checkpoint: post one station graph or photo and explain the force pattern it reveals, including one limitation.

scenes.label: Predict
scenes.title: Four events—three hidden patterns
scenes.prompt: Watch the quick cases. Group them by what stays the same, what changes, and which objects interact.
scenes.studentTask: A before-and-after grouping with one reason

scenes.label: Investigate
scenes.title: Rotate through the force stations
scenes.prompt: At each station, change one condition, repeat the test, and record a pattern—not just a result.
scenes.studentTask: Four station records and one graph

scenes.label: Test
scenes.title: Can a digital model reproduce the pattern?
scenes.prompt: Use three PhET challenges to test your station claims. Record where the model agrees and what it simplifies.
scenes.studentTask: Three model cases and one limitation

scenes.label: Teach
scenes.title: Make one law useful
scenes.prompt: Teach a new case using an object, force arrows, evidence, and one Newton pattern. Your classmates should do some thinking.
scenes.studentTask: A two-minute interactive explanation

resources.label: STEMonstrations: Newton's Second Law
resources.task: Record the pattern shown when the same kind of push acts on objects with different mass.
resources.support: Pause before each astronaut demonstration and have students predict which object will change motion more.

resources.label: Forces and Motion: Basics
resources.task: Create one balanced case, one unbalanced case, and one same-force/different-mass case; screenshot or sketch each.
resources.support: Use only Net Force, Motion, and Friction. Work through the three assigned challenges rather than free play first.

lessons.title: Crash Lab
lessons.question: How does padding change the force during a sudden stop?
lessons.learning: We are using repeated evidence to explain why a longer, less sudden stop can reduce peak force without making force disappear.
success: I make a hypothesis with a scientific reason.
I change one variable and run repeated trials.
I graph and compare stopping-time and peak-force evidence.
I identify a model limitation.
lessons.inquiry: Compare no padding, thin foam, and thick foam while mass and speed stay fixed; use repeated results to decide which explanation is best supported.
lessons.reflection: What does the model show clearly, and what real-world safety factors does it leave out?
lessons.exit: Use a measured result to explain how foam changed stopping time and peak force.
lessons.evidence: A hypothesis, nine-trial table, comparison graph, CER conclusion, and model limitation
lessons.projectContribution: A complete fair-test and data-analysis rehearsal for the Delivery Pod explanation.
lessons.spacesPrompt: Checkpoint option: post the comparison graph and a claim–evidence–reasoning explanation of how padding changed the stop.

scenes.label: Notice
scenes.title: A passenger does not stop by magic
scenes.prompt: Predict belt versus no belt, replay the stop, and identify the interaction that changes the passenger's motion.
scenes.studentTask: A prediction, observation, and labelled force diagram

scenes.label: Investigate
scenes.title: One changed variable, nine simulated trials
scenes.prompt: Lock mass and speed. Change only padding and collect three model outputs for every condition.
scenes.studentTask: A nine-trial model-data table and calculated averages

scenes.label: Explain
scenes.title: Graph how the stop changes
scenes.prompt: Compare stopping time and peak force together. Explain the mechanism rather than only naming the safest bar.
scenes.studentTask: A two-variable comparison graph and mechanism notes

scenes.label: Conclude
scenes.title: Make the data do the talking
scenes.prompt: Write or record a claim, cite repeated evidence, explain why it fits, and name one model limit.
scenes.studentTask: A checkpoint-ready CER explanation

resources.label: Newton's laws of motion
resources.task: Connect inertia to the passenger or package continuing forward during a sudden stop.
resources.support: Use the first-law diagram and plain-language summary only; skip equations and aerospace calculations.

lessons.title: Forces in human movement
lessons.question: How do forces help a body start, stop, jump, land, and change direction?
lessons.learning: We are applying force patterns to movement without grading athletic ability or asking anyone to perform beyond their comfort.
success: I identify the object and interaction for each force arrow.
I explain how the ground can push on a person.
I compare a stable and unstable landing using evidence.
I communicate one movement cue accurately and respectfully.
lessons.inquiry: Analyse a jump, landing, wheelchair push, ball kick, or quick direction change frame by frame; identify interactions and revise one coaching claim.
lessons.reflection: How can a movement cue be scientifically useful without pretending every body moves in exactly the same way?
lessons.exit: Use two force arrows and one Newton pattern to explain one moment of movement.
lessons.evidence: An annotated movement sequence, two interaction pairs, and one revised science-based coaching explanation
lessons.projectContribution: A cross-curricular application showing how the same force patterns operate in sport, dance, play, and mobility.

scenes.label: Observe
scenes.title: Freeze the instant when motion changes
scenes.prompt: Compare two slow-motion cases. Describe what changes before naming the force.
scenes.studentTask: Three frame-by-frame observations

scenes.label: Map
scenes.title: Which object pushes which?
scenes.prompt: Add force arrows to the person or object, then pair every interaction with the force on the other object.
scenes.learningMode: Force-frame annotation · Crash Course Kids clip
scenes.studentTask: Two annotated frames and two interaction pairs

scenes.label: Test
scenes.title: Change one movement condition safely
scenes.prompt: Compare an object, seated, standing, or video case. Change one condition and collect evidence about stability, friction, or stopping.
scenes.studentTask: A safe comparison and one evidence note

scenes.label: Communicate
scenes.title: Turn a slogan into an explanation
scenes.prompt: Repair a vague coaching claim so it names the interaction, evidence, and limits.
scenes.studentTask: A revised coaching explanation for a Grade 6 audience

resources.label: Defining Gravity
resources.task: Add gravity to the force frame and explain why it still acts while an object is moving upward.
resources.support: Pause before the falling examples. Ask students to draw gravity on the moving person or object rather than merely repeat the definition.

lessons.title: Delivery Pod STEM Challenge
lessons.question: How high can your pod fall and still protect its egg—and how will you prove why?
lessons.learning: We are applying force and impact evidence through a fair design cycle, visible revision, and clear communication.
success: Our design follows the common constraints.
We use Crash Lab evidence to justify a feature.
We measure tests and make one visible revision.
Each person can explain the science and a limitation.
lessons.inquiry: Design one pod, complete a controlled practice drop, inspect evidence, revise one feature, and enter the height ladder or equivalent measured test.
lessons.reflection: Which result changed your team's thinking, and what would you test next?
lessons.exit: Explain one feature using force, stopping time or motion evidence—and name what the test cannot prove.
lessons.evidence: Team prototype and results, one visible revision, and an individual evidence-based explanation
lessons.projectContribution: A complete portfolio highlight and a possible Forces topic for later expert-team inquiry.
lessons.spacesPrompt: Portfolio highlight: post the team design photo or Minecraft model, results table, and an individual explanation of one design decision, evidence, revision, and next step.

scenes.label: Frame
scenes.title: A fair challenge, not a mystery craft
scenes.prompt: Inspect the criteria, constraints, common kit, and evidence from Crash Lab. Choose the mechanism your first design will use.
scenes.studentTask: A labelled sketch with one mechanism claim

scenes.label: Build
scenes.title: Build the claim into the pod
scenes.prompt: Construct one design. Every material must have a job connected to the sketch.
scenes.studentTask: A constraint-compliant prototype

scenes.label: Test
scenes.title: One practice drop, one visible revision
scenes.prompt: Measure the practice height, observe what happened, and change one feature for a stated reason.
scenes.studentTask: Practice result and documented revision

scenes.label: Challenge
scenes.title: Climb the height ladder safely
scenes.prompt: Enter the measured challenge or equivalent test. Record every result, including useful failures.
scenes.studentTask: Final measured result and class comparison

scenes.label: Explain
scenes.title: Prove more than survival
scenes.prompt: Use the design, data, and revision to explain what likely helped, what remains uncertain, and what you would test next.
scenes.studentTask: Portfolio-ready individual explanation

title: Earth & Space
subtitle: A truthful cosmic tour
question: How can we show our place in the universe without fooling people about scale and motion?
bigIdea: The solar system is part of the Milky Way, which is one of billions of galaxies.
content: Scale and structure of the universe
assessment: Create an evidence-based cosmic tour that communicates scale, structure, motion, and model limits.

lessons.title: You are here
lessons.question: Where exactly are we in the universe—and how can a model show it honestly?
lessons.learning: We are building Earth's nested cosmic address and using more than one model because no single model can show size, distance, structure, and time accurately at once.
success: I can order Earth, solar system, Milky Way, and observable universe.
I can use a scale to place several planets at defensible distances.
I can explain what a model shows well and what it distorts.
I can use light-travel time to explain why looking far away also means looking into the past.
lessons.inquiry: Build and revise three complementary models: a nested cosmic address, a distance-only solar-system walk, and a 13.8-metre timeline of the universe.
lessons.reflection: Why do scientists need several different models for the same universe?
lessons.exit: Write Earth's cosmic address and one precise warning for each model: what is accurate, what is enlarged, and what is left out.
lessons.evidence: A revised cosmic address, measured distance model, cosmic timeline annotation, and two accurate model-limit statements
lessons.projectContribution: Students practise turning an enormous idea into a truthful model; they may save a space question without choosing their final expert-team topic.

scenes.label: Address
scenes.title: Put our cosmic address in order
scenes.prompt: Arrange the five places from smallest to largest. Keep your first answer visible so NASA evidence can make you revise it.
scenes.studentTask: A before-and-after cosmic address with one quoted or paraphrased piece of NASA evidence

scenes.label: Locate
scenes.title: Our solar system is not at the centre
scenes.prompt: Use a trusted map and description to locate the solar system in the Milky Way, then explain why most galaxy diagrams cannot be photographs from outside our galaxy.
scenes.studentTask: A labelled Milky Way sketch and one inference about how the model was constructed

scenes.label: Measure
scenes.title: Walk a distance-only solar system
scenes.prompt: Place each planet at a measured distance from the Sun. Then catch the trick: are the planet markers also the correct size?
scenes.studentTask: Planet placements, one checked distance calculation, and a visible model-limit warning

scenes.label: Time
scenes.title: Turn 13.8 billion years into 13.8 metres
scenes.prompt: Place cosmic events on a timeline. Then use light-travel time to explain why distant space is also ancient evidence.
scenes.studentTask: A timeline annotation and a two-sentence explanation linking distance, light, and the past

resources.label: What Is a Galaxy?
resources.task: Find two sentences that prove a solar system is smaller than a galaxy, then revise the group card sort.
resources.support: Read the short answer and the diagram captions; the full page is optional.

resources.label: Solar System Facts
resources.task: Confirm where our solar system sits in the Milky Way and record one fact that changes your mental picture.
resources.support: Use the introduction and Our Place in the Milky Way section; do not assign the entire page.

resources.label: Eyes on the Solar System
resources.task: Compare the compressed screen view with the 45 m walk. Identify one distance or size the screen must distort.
resources.support: Demonstrate navigation first and work in pairs; the goal is model critique, not visiting every object.

resources.label: What Is a Light-Year?
resources.task: Explain why a telescope can show both far-away space and the past.
resources.support: Read through the Looking Back in Time section and stop before the more advanced examples if needed.

resources.label: What Is the Big Bang?
resources.task: Place the age of the universe on the timeline and identify one piece of evidence described in the article.
resources.support: Use it as a supported partner reading; distinguish expansion from an explosion at one location.

lessons.title: Patterns in motion
lessons.question: How can the same motion look different from Earth and from space?
lessons.learning: We are using rotation, revolution, orbit, gravity, and viewpoint to explain repeating patterns without confusing observation with explanation.
success: I can distinguish an observation from an explanation.
I can model how rotation causes day and night.
I can compare planetary day and year data and identify an anomaly.
I can explain how viewpoint changes apparent motion and name a model limit.
lessons.inquiry: Collect or examine sky-pattern evidence, build a physical Sun–Earth model, compare planetary data, and use a digital model to test which explanation fits all observations.
lessons.reflection: Which idea became clearer only after you changed viewpoint or changed models?
lessons.exit: Explain day and night, distinguish a day from a year, and name one thing the model exaggerates or leaves out.
lessons.evidence: An observation/explanation sort, physical-model diagram, planetary-data comparison, and viewpoint-based explanation
lessons.projectContribution: Students practise using several forms of evidence and may save a motion question without committing to a final inquiry topic.

scenes.label: Observe
scenes.title: The sky seems to turn—but what does that prove?
scenes.prompt: Study a time-lapse or shadow sequence. Record only visible changes first, then list at least two possible explanations.
scenes.studentTask: Two-column observation/explanation notes and one question the evidence cannot answer alone

scenes.label: Model
scenes.title: Carry Surrey from day into night
scenes.prompt: Use a fixed light and rotating Earth. Track Surrey through sunrise, noon, sunset, and midnight, then draw the view from space and the view from the ground.
scenes.learningMode: Human model · lamp investigation · dual-view diagram
scenes.studentTask: A four-position day/night diagram and a cause-and-effect explanation

scenes.label: Compare
scenes.title: Every planet has a day and a year—but not like ours
scenes.prompt: Graph planetary rotation and revolution data. Find a pattern, an outlier, and one question the data raises.
scenes.studentTask: Two graphs or tables, one supported pattern, one anomaly, and one new question

scenes.label: Viewpoint
scenes.title: Change where you stand; change what appears to move
scenes.prompt: Compare the same system from Earth and from space. Choose the explanation that fits both views and identify a limit of every model used.
scenes.studentTask: A corrected explanation of apparent motion using rotation, viewpoint, and one named model limit

resources.label: Move like the Earth and the Moon
resources.task: Use the Earth–Sun movement steps to check your group's physical model, then identify one way your model is not to scale.
resources.support: Use the rotation and Earth-revolution sections; Moon phases and eclipses are optional extensions, not core tasks.

resources.label: How Long Is One Day on Other Planets?
resources.task: Graph the six comparable planets, then explain why Mercury and Venus need a different graph scale.
resources.support: The page models moving from paragraph to table to graph, making it suitable for a Science–Math connection.

resources.label: Eyes on the Solar System
resources.task: Change viewpoint and compare what appears to move. Capture one observation and one explanation without treating the animation as perfectly to scale.
resources.support: Demonstrate controls first; pairs investigate one assigned viewpoint rather than exploring without a purpose.

lessons.title: Cosmic exhibit studio
lessons.question: Can you teach one cosmic idea clearly without making the model lie?
lessons.learning: We are communicating one cosmic idea with accurate structure, evidence, citations, and an honest statement of model limits.
success: Our exhibit teaches one focused idea.
Every important claim is supported by a trusted source.
Our visual accurately shows structure or motion and labels deliberate distortions.
Peer feedback leads to a visible revision.
lessons.inquiry: Choose one bounded cosmic story, research it with two trusted sources, build a physical, digital, or Minecraft museum stop, peer-audit it, revise, and teach it in two minutes.
lessons.reflection: Which revision most improved truthfulness or understanding—and what evidence caused that revision?
lessons.exit: Point to one deliberate distortion, explain why it was necessary, and name the source that keeps the exhibit accurate.
lessons.evidence: Focused question, source notes, draft exhibit, peer audit, visible revision, two-minute teaching, and individual reflection
lessons.projectContribution: A rehearsal for expert-team teaching and one optional Earth & Space topic to keep in the SpacesEDU Topic Bank; it does not lock students into a final topic.

scenes.label: Audit
scenes.title: Find the five beautiful mistakes
scenes.prompt: Inspect the display before opening the answers. Classify each problem as structure, scale, motion, evidence, or a missing warning.
scenes.studentTask: A five-part audit with corrections and the source needed to verify each one

scenes.label: Focus
scenes.title: Choose one story worth teaching
scenes.prompt: Turn a broad space topic into one learning goal your audience can understand in two minutes, then locate two approved sources that serve different purposes.
scenes.studentTask: One-sentence learning goal, two source notes, and a plan naming the visual evidence

scenes.label: Build
scenes.title: Build the explanation before the decoration
scenes.prompt: Create the core model, citation, and 'This model distorts…' warning. Ask another team to test whether the explanation works before polishing it.
scenes.learningMode: Team creation · mid-build check · peer test
scenes.studentTask: A teachable draft containing one accurate model, two citations, and one specific model warning

scenes.label: Teach
scenes.title: Peer-audit, revise, and open the museum
scenes.prompt: Use the checklist on another exhibit, make one visible revision, and teach your museum stop in two minutes. Save a possible topic only if it still interests you.
scenes.learningMode: Peer critique · revision · museum walk · reflection
scenes.studentTask: Completed peer audit, revised exhibit, two-minute teaching, and optional Space topic-bank entry

resources.label: Solar System Facts
resources.task: Use the page to verify or reject two claims in the flawed exhibit. Record the heading where the evidence appears.
resources.support: Assign different claims to different teams; students do not need to read the whole page.

resources.label: Universe
resources.task: Choose one article that can support a focused exhibit question, then write the exact idea it will help you teach.
resources.support: Use the menu as a curated starting point, not as permission to browse randomly.

resources.label: Educational videos
resources.task: Filter for Grades 4–6 and select one short clip only if it adds evidence or a useful visual your other source lacks.
resources.support: Teacher previews the chosen clip; students must name its purpose before watching.

resources.label: NASA Image and Video Library
resources.task: Choose one accurately captioned image and record its title, credit, and what it can—and cannot—prove.
resources.support: Search using the approved topic phrase; require the original caption and credit rather than copying an unlabelled image.
